report:
Conclusion: the claim is **not supported** for ordinary cloth or surgical masks. The best evidence and public-health guidance agree that properly worn medical/cloth masks do **not** cause dangerous CO₂ intoxication or oxygen deficiency; exhaled CO₂ passes through and around loose-fitting masks, and any rise inside the mask’s small dead space does not translate into clinically meaningful blood CO₂ in healthy people. WHO states plainly that prolonged medical-mask use “DOES NOT cause CO2 intoxication nor oxygen deficiency” (https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public/myth-busters). A direct gas-exchange study of healthy adults and COPD patients wearing surgical masks found no clinically important oxygen/CO₂ impairment (https://www.atsjournals.org/doi/10.1513/AnnalsATS.202007-812RL?cookieSet=1). BBC’s expert review likewise says CO₂ is “unlikely to build up” enough to harm (https://www.bbc.com/news/53108405), and AP notes claims that CDC said cloth masks trap CO₂ are false (https://apnews.com/article/archive-fact-checking-9101740032).

Caveats: masks can feel hot, humid, uncomfortable, or anxiety-provoking; take breaks when safe. People with severe cardiopulmonary disease, those doing intense exercise, and anyone using tight respirators for long shifts should seek individualized advice; infants under 2 should not wear masks. But “dangerous CO₂ buildup” from routine cloth/surgical mask use is a myth.
